note: Rabbi Akiva once picked the fruit of an etrog tree on the first day of the month of Shevat. He set aside two different tithes from it: one as if the new year for trees had already begun, following Beit Shammai, and one as if it had not, following Beit Hillel.
why: The mishna gives the first of Shevat as the new year for trees according to Beit Shammai, while Beit Hillel say the fifteenth. Rabbi Akiva's double tithe shows him unwilling to decide between them; Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda then says his doubt was really between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and, unsure which year it belonged to, set aside two tithes from it.

terms.meaning: A citron, a lemon-like fruit; its tree has some rules of a tree and some of a vegetable.
A tenth of produce set aside for a religious purpose. Which tithe is due depends on the year of a seven-year cycle: second tithe in some years, poor man's tithe in others.
The schools of two early Sages, Shammai and Hillel, who disagree on many points of law.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.
